query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, reactive nickel coating to tungsten particles prior to copper infusion will promote an in situ, graded interfacial alloy during spark-plasma sintering that minimizes void formation and enhances both thermal transport and mechanical durability relative to vapor‐coated tungsten powders processed without such a coating.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite of tungsten particles (or connected tungsten regions) embedded in a copper matrix, where tungsten surfaces are unmodified (bare) as conventionally processed.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin nickel coating on tungsten particles before copper infusion and subsequent spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Sintering under controlled temperature (well below tungsten’s melting point of ~3422 °C and below copper’s boiling point of ~2562 °C) and pressure conditions typical for spark plasma sintering; service conditions mimic fusion-reactor heat transfer joints under irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: A graded interfacial alloy layer formed at the tungsten–copper boundary through the reactive interaction of the nickel coating with copper during sintering.
generation.mechanism: The nickel coating reacts during sintering with the copper to form a localized intermetallic or solid solution, which improves wetting between the phases, suppresses void formation, and strengthens interfacial bonding—thereby both enhancing thermal conductivity and maintaining mechanical durability under demanding conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nickel-coated tungsten composites should exhibit lower interfacial void content, reduced thermal interface resistance, and improved mechanical integrity (e.g., higher tensile strength and fatigue resistance) compared to the baseline process that employs vapor-coated tungsten powders.
generation.baseline: Current vapor-coated tungsten powders sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between tungsten and copper without the introduction of a reactive interlayer.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable under spark plasma sintering conditions for W–Cu composites used in fusion reactor heat transfer joints, with effectiveness assessed before significant irradiation exposure.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thickness of the nickel coating and its long-term behavior under actual irradiation conditions remain uncertain. The exact extent of interfacial alloy formation and its influence on overall composite performance need further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one with tungsten particles pre-coated with a thin nickel film and one control set without the nickel coating, using identical spark plasma sintering parameters. Simulate operational conditions including thermal cycling and irradiation in lab tests.
measurements: High-resolution microscopy (TEM/SEM) to quantify void content and inspect interfacial morphology
Thermal conductivity measurements to assess improvements in heat transport
Mechanical tests (tensile strength, fatigue resistance) to evaluate durability before and after simulated irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nickel-coated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in void reduction, thermal conductivity, or mechanical durability compared to the control set, or if the nickel coating introduces adverse effects under irradiation, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
